yielding

ℙ[lossyWLv(G)⊨𝒢𝒱fv(G)]>0\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash_{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}f_{v}({G})]>0

Now we show that from WLv(G)⊭𝒢𝒱fv(G){\textup{WL}}_{v}({G})\nvDash_{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}f_{v}({G}), it follows that ℙ[lossyWLv(G)⊨𝒢𝒱fv(G)]=0\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash_{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}f_{v}({G})]=0, i.e., losing messages cannot make the probabilistic WL test more expressive than the deterministic WL test. WLv​(G)⊭fv​(G){\textup{WL}}_{v}({G})\nvDash f_{v}({G}) implies there is G′,w∈𝒢𝒱{G}^{\prime},w\in{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}} with WLv​(G)=WLw​(G′){\textup{WL}}_{v}({G})={\textup{WL}}_{w}({G}^{\prime}) but fv​(G)≠fw​(G′)f_{v}({G})\neq f_{w}({G}^{\prime}). Then, for every seed s1∈Ss_{1}\in S, there exists a seed s2∈Ss_{2}\in S such that

lossyWLv​(G,s1)=lossyWLw​(G′,s2).\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G},s_{1})=\textup{lossyWL}_{w}({G}^{\prime},s_{2}).

(the same messages to WL equivalent nodes in G{G} and G′{G}^{\prime} are lost). Hence by Definition 4.4,

ℙ(lossyWLv(G)⊨𝒢𝒱fv(G))=0.∎\mathbb{P}(\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash_{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}f_{v}({G}))=0.\qed

Using this, we can prove when MPC becomes infinite:

See 4.6

Proof.

Assume first that there exists G,v∈𝒢𝒱{G},v\in{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}} with MPCℳS​(f,G)=∞{\textup{MPC}}_{{\mathcal{M}}_{S}}(f,{G})=\infty. By definition, this implies that

ℙ[lossyWLv(G)⊨𝒢𝒱fv(G)]=0.\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash_{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}f_{v}({G})]=0.

From Lemma C.6 it follows that

WLv(G)⊭𝒢𝒱fv(G).{\textup{WL}}_{v}({G})\nvDash_{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}f_{v}({G}).

By definition of ⊨\vDash this implies that there exists G′,w∈𝒢𝒱{G}^{\prime},w\in{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}} with WLv​(G)=WLw​(G′){\textup{WL}}_{v}({G})={\textup{WL}}_{w}({G}^{\prime}) but fv​(G)≠fw​(G′)f_{v}({G})\neq f_{w}({G}^{\prime}). Now it follows from the fact that the WL test upper-bounds the expressivity of standard MPNNs ℳS{{\mathcal{M}}_{S}} [36] that also all models M∈ℳM\in{\mathcal{M}} cannot differentiate G,v{G},v from G′,w{G}^{\prime},w, i.e., Mv​(G)=Mw​(G′)M_{v}({G})=M_{w}({G}^{\prime}).

Now, assume that MPCℳS​(f,G)≠∞{\textup{MPC}}_{{\mathcal{M}}_{S}}(f,{G})\neq\infty. By definition, this implies that

ℙ[lossyWLv(G)⊨𝒢𝒱fv(G)]>0.\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash_{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}f_{v}({G})]>0.

From Lemma C.6 it follows that

WLv(G)⊨𝒢𝒱fv(G).{\textup{WL}}_{v}({G})\vDash_{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}f_{v}({G}).

By definition of ⊨\vDash this implies that there do not exist G′,w∈𝒢𝒱{G}^{\prime},w\in{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}} with WLv​(G)=WLw​(G′){\textup{WL}}_{v}({G})={\textup{WL}}_{w}({G}^{\prime}) but fv​(G)≠fw​(G′)f_{v}({G})\neq f_{w}({G}^{\prime}). Now note that by Lemma C.5 there exists a model M∈ℳSM\in{{\mathcal{M}}_{S}} performing exactly the WL test. Hence, there exists M∈ℳS{M}\in{{\mathcal{M}}_{S}} such that there does not exist G′,w∈𝒢𝒱{G}^{\prime},w\in{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}} with Mv​(G)=Mw​(G′){M}_{v}({G})={M}_{w}({G}^{\prime}) but fv​(G)≠fw​(G′)f_{v}({G})\neq f_{w}({G}^{\prime}). ∎

With this, we can also globally characterize which functions an MPNN can express:

See 4.7

Proof.

If there exists M∈ℳ{M}\in{\mathcal{M}} such that Mv​(G)=fv​(G){M}_{v}({G})=f_{v}({G}) for all G,v∈𝒢𝒱{G},v\in{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}, it follows directly from Thm. 4.6 that there does not exist G,v∈𝒢𝒱{G},v\in{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}} with MPCℳS​(fv,G)=∞{\textup{MPC}}_{{\mathcal{M}}_{S}}(f_{v},{G})=\infty.

If there does not exist G,v∈𝒢𝒱{G},v\in{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}} with MPCℳS​(fv,G)=∞{\textup{MPC}}_{{\mathcal{M}}_{S}}(f_{v},{G})=\infty, this implies that for all G,v∈𝒢𝒱{G},v\in{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}

ℙ[lossyWLv(G)⊨𝒢𝒱fv(G)]>0.\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash_{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}f_{v}({G})]>0.

Hence, by Lemma C.6 for all G,v∈𝒢𝒱{G},v\in{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}

WLv(G)⊨𝒢𝒱fv(G).{\textup{WL}}_{v}({G})\vDash_{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}f_{v}({G}).

So

WL⊨𝒢𝒱f.{\textup{WL}}\vDash_{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}f.

By Lemma C.5 there exists M∈ℳSM\in{{\mathcal{M}}_{S}} with M⊨𝒢𝒱fM\vDash_{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}f. And by Lemma C.4 a function τ\tau such that for all G,v∈𝒢𝒱{G},v\in{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}

τ∘Mv​(G)=fv​(G).\tau\circ M_{v}({G})=f_{v}({G}).

But then we can squash the function τ\tau also in the last update layer of M{M}, i.e., updnewl=τ∘updl{\texttt{upd}}_{\text{new}}^{l}=\tau\circ{\texttt{upd}}^{l}. With this, we have found a model M∗{M}^{*} such that

Mv∗​(G)=fv​(G)M^{*}_{v}({G})=f_{v}({G})

for all G,v∈𝒢𝒱{G},v\in{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}. ∎

As a special case, we can recover the iso expressivity statements defined in Definition 3.1. For this, we use the graph-level formulation of MPC. Note that all previous theorems generalize completely analogously also to this graph-level version.

Lemma C.7 (MPC preserves impossibility statement of Iso Expressivity).

Let α\alpha be a graph isomorphism test. Then ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is at least as expressive as α\alpha if and only if there does not exist G∈𝒢∗{G}\in{\mathcal{G}}^{*} with MPC(α,G)ℳ=∞{\textup{MPC}}{}_{\mathcal{M}}(\alpha,G)=\infty.

Proof.

If MPC(α,G)ℳ=∞{\textup{MPC}}{}_{\mathcal{M}}(\alpha,{G})=\infty for some G∈𝒢∗{G}\in{\mathcal{G}}^{*}, then by Thm. 4.6, there exists G′∈𝒢∗{G}^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{G}}^{*} such that M⁡(G)=M⁡(G′){M}({G})={M}({G}^{\prime}) for all M∈ℳ{M}\in{\mathcal{M}} but α⁡(G)≠α⁡(G′)\alpha({G})\neq\alpha({G}^{\prime}). From this follows directly that ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is not at least as expressive as α\alpha.

Now assume that there does not exist G∈𝒢∗{G}\in{\mathcal{G}}^{*} with MPC(α,G)ℳ=∞{\textup{MPC}}{}_{\mathcal{M}}(\alpha,{G})=\infty. Then by Lemma 4.7 there exists M∈ℳM\in{\mathcal{M}} with M⁡(G)=α⁡(G)M({G})=\alpha({G}) for all G∈𝒢∗{G}\in{\mathcal{G}}^{*}. Therefore, ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is at least as expressive as α\alpha. ∎

C.4 Bounding MPC: Function Refinement & Compositionality

Next, we will prove bounds on MPC relating to how fine-grained a task is and how it can be decomposed into individual subtasks. First, we prove that a more fine-grained function cannot have lower complexity than the coarser function it refines: See 4.8

Proof.

The intuitive idea for this proof is that if the set of successful messages in lossyWL suffices to deduce ff, it is also always possible to deduce the more coarse-grained gg.

First, note that ⊨\vDash is transitive. Then, it follows directly that for every seed s∈Ss\in S for which lossyWLv(G,s)⊨𝒢𝒱×Sfv\textup{lossyWL}_{v}(G,s)\vDash_{{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}\times S}f_{v} also lossyWLv(G,s)⊨𝒢𝒱×Sgv\textup{lossyWL}_{v}(G,s)\vDash_{{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}\times S}g_{v}. Therefore

ℙ[lossyWLv(G)⊨𝒢𝒱fv(G)]≤ℙ[lossyWLv(G)⊨𝒢𝒱gv(G)].\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash_{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}f_{v}({G})]\leq\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash_{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}g_{v}({G})].

And hence,

MPCℳ​(fv,G)≥MPCℳ​(gv,G).∎{\textup{MPC}}_{\mathcal{M}}(f_{v},{G})\geq{\textup{MPC}}_{\mathcal{M}}(g_{v},{G}).\qed

Now, we will prove the compositional property of MPC. See 4.9

Proof.

Let LfL_{f} be a sufficient set of messages for fvf_{v} on graph GG. Let 𝕃f{\mathbb{L}}_{f} denote the set of all such sufficient sets LfL_{f}. Notice that 𝕃f{\mathbb{L}}_{f} is upward-closed, i.e., any superset of a Lf∈𝕃fL_{f}\in{\mathbb{L}}_{f} is also sufficient and therefore in 𝕃f{\mathbb{L}}_{f}. This intuitively means that more successful messages cannot hurt. Define analogously 𝕃g{\mathbb{L}}_{g} for the task gg.

For a set of messages SS define αf(S)=𝟏[S∈𝕃f]\alpha_{f}(S)=\mathbf{1}[S\in{\mathbb{L}}_{f}]. Then, αf\alpha_{f} is an increasing function over sets, i.e., S⊆S′⟹αf​(S)≤αf​(S′)S\subseteq S^{\prime}\implies\alpha_{f}(S)\leq\alpha_{f}(S^{\prime}), because 𝕃f{\mathbb{L}}_{f} is upward-closed. From the Fortuin–Kasteleyn–Ginibre (FKG) inequality, we then have (where SS follows the distributions of the sets of successful messages in lossyWL):

𝔼⁡[αf​(S)​αg​(S)]≥𝔼⁡[αf​(S)]⋅𝔼⁡[αg​(S)]\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{f}(S)\alpha_{g}(S)]\geq\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{f}(S)]\cdot\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{g}(S)]

implying

ℙ[lossyWLv(G)⊨fv(G)∧lossyWLv(G)⊨gv(G)]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash f_{v}({G})\land\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash g_{v}({G})]
≥ℙ[lossyWLv(G)⊨fv(G)]⋅ℙ[lossyWLv(G)⊨gv(G)]\displaystyle\quad\geq\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash f_{v}({G})]\cdot\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash g_{v}({G})]

and thereby

MPCℳ(fv∥gv,G)≤MPCℳ(fv,G)+MPCℳ(gv,G).∎{\textup{MPC}}_{\mathcal{M}}(f_{v}\|g_{v},{G})\leq{\textup{MPC}}_{\mathcal{M}}(f_{v},{G})+{\textup{MPC}}_{\mathcal{M}}(g_{v},{G}).\qed

C.5 Connection of MPC to Over-squashing and Under-reaching

To formalize Lemma 4.10, we first need to define when a task fvf_{v} requires information from another node uu.

Definition C.8.

We say a task fvf_{v} over graphs 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} requires (node-feature) information from a node uu if there exists G1,G2∈𝒢{G}^{1},{G}^{2}\in{\mathcal{G}} that are identical except for the node features 𝑿u1≠𝑿u2{\bm{X}}^{1}_{u}\neq{\bm{X}}_{u}^{2} and

fv​(G1)≠fv​(G2).f_{v}({G}^{1})\neq f_{v}({G}^{2}).

So a task requires information from a node uu, if without this information it would be impossible to compute fvf_{v}.

With this in place, we can give a formal version of Lemma 4.10:

Lemma C.9.

Consider a task fvf_{v} and a graph G∈𝒢{G}\in{\mathcal{G}} where fvf_{v} requires node-feature information from uu. Then

MPCℳ​(fv,G)≥−log⁡((𝑰L)v​u).{\textup{MPC}}_{\mathcal{M}}(f_{v},{G})\geq-\log\left(({{\bm{I}}}^{L})_{vu}\right).
Proof.

Intuitively, we will show that in order to deduce fvf_{v} from lossyWLv\textup{lossyWL}_{v} there needs to exist an L-length walk from uu to vv where all messages were successful (as fvf_{v} requires information from uu). The probability of this can be in turn upperbounded by the random walk probability.

Formally, we need to show that

ℙ[lossyWLv(G)⊨fv(G)]≤(𝑰L)v​u.\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash f_{v}({G})]\leq({{\bm{I}}}^{L})_{vu}.

For this we will upper bound ℙ[lossyWLv(G)⊨fv(G)]\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash f_{v}({G})] by the LL step random walk probability from vv to uu.

For this, let Wa​bW_{ab} be the event that there exists x1,…​xL−1∈𝒱Gx_{1},\dots x_{L-1}\in{\mathcal{V}_{G}} with

Za​x11=1∧Zx1​x22=1∧Zx2​x33=1∧⋯∧ZxL−2​xL−1L−1=1∧ZxL−1​bL=1.Z_{ax_{1}}^{1}=1\land Z_{x_{1}x_{2}}^{2}=1\land Z^{3}_{x_{2}x_{3}}=1\land\dots\land Z^{L-1}_{x_{L-2}x_{L-1}}=1\land Z^{L}_{x_{L-1}b}=1.

We then say ZZ contains a (LL-length) walk from aa to bb. Additionally, let Wa​biW_{ab}^{i} be the event that ZZ contains a specific walk from aa to bb with fully specified intermediate nodes xjx_{j}. Then the probability of Wa​biW_{ab}^{i} is (using the independence of the variables ZZ):

ℙ⁡[Wa​bi]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[W_{ab}^{i}] =ℙ[Za​x11=1]⋅ℙ[Zx1​x22=1]⋯ℙ[ZxL−1​bL=1]\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}[Z^{1}_{ax_{1}}=1]\cdot\mathbb{P}[Z_{x_{1}x_{2}}^{2}=1]\cdots\mathbb{P}[Z_{x_{L-1}b}^{L}=1]
=𝑰x1​a⋅𝑰x2​x1⋯𝑰b​xL−1\displaystyle={{\bm{I}}}_{x_{1}a}\cdot{{\bm{I}}}_{x_{2}x_{1}}\cdots{{\bm{I}}}_{bx_{L-1}}

This is precisely the probability for a random walk from bb to aa over all intermediate nodes xix_{i} with edge probabilities 𝑰{{\bm{I}}}. If we now consider all LL-length walks Wa​b1,…,Wa​bkW_{ab}^{1},\dots,W_{ab}^{k} from aa to bb, we get:

ℙ⁡[Wa​b]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[W_{ab}] ≤ℙ⁡[Wa​b1]+⋯+ℙ⁡[Wa​bk]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}[W^{1}_{ab}]+\cdots+\mathbb{P}[W_{ab}^{k}]
=ℙ⁡[L-step random walk from b to a with edge probabilities 𝑰]\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}[\text{$L$-step random walk from $b$ to $a$ with edge probabilities ${{\bm{I}}}$}]
=(𝑰L)b​a\displaystyle=({{\bm{I}}}^{L})_{ba}

Now note that if not Wu​vW_{uv}, i.e., ZZ contains no walk from uu to vv, it is by Definition C.8 not possible to deduce fv​(G)f_{v}({G}) from lossyWLv​(G)\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G}) as vv will not receive any information from uu.

Hence,

ℙ[lossyWL(G)v⊨fv(G)]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}({G})_{v}\vDash f_{v}({G})] ≤ℙ⁡[Wu​v]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}[W_{uv}]
≤(𝑰L)v​u∎.\displaystyle\leq({{\bm{I}}}^{L})_{vu}\qed.

With this we can easily prove Corollary 4.11:

Proof.

If dG​(u,v)>Ld_{G}(u,v)>L there exists no LL step walk from vv to uu on G{G}. Therefore (𝑰L)v​u=0({{\bm{I}}}^{L})_{vu}=0 and by definition of MPC:

MPCℳ​(fv,G)=∞.{\textup{MPC}}_{\mathcal{M}}(f_{v},{G})=\infty.

∎

C.6 Complexity bounds in § 5

First, we will prove two useful lemmas to upper and lower bound the MPC complexities:

Lemma C.10.

Let 𝕊{\mathbb{S}} be a sufficient set of messages for a function fvf_{v} on a graph G{G}. Then

MPCℳ​(fv,G)≤−log⁡(ℙ⁡[𝕊]).{\textup{MPC}}_{\mathcal{M}}(f_{v},{G})\leq-\log(\mathbb{P}[{\mathbb{S}}]).
Proof.

By Definition C.1 we have:

ℙ[lossyWLv(t(G))⊨fv(G)]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}(t({G}))\vDash f_{v}({G})] ≥ℙ[⋀(a,b,l)∈𝕊Za​bl=1]\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{P}[\bigwedge_{(a,b,l)\in{\mathbb{S}}}Z_{ab}^{l}=1]
=ℙ⁡[𝕊]∎\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}[{\mathbb{S}}]\qed

And a corresponding lower bound:

Lemma C.11.

Let 𝕊{\mathbb{S}} be a necessary set of messages for a function fvf_{v} on a graph G{G}. Then

MPC​(ℳ,fv,G)≥−log⁡(ℙ⁡[𝕊]).{\textup{MPC}}({\mathcal{M}},f_{v},{G})\geq-\log(\mathbb{P}[{\mathbb{S}}]).
Proof.

It follows directly from Definition C.2 that

ℙ[lossyWLv(t(G))⊨fv(G)]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}(t({G}))\vDash f_{v}({G})] ≤ℙ[⋀(a,b,l)∈𝕊Za​bl=1]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}[\bigwedge_{(a,b,l)\in{\mathbb{S}}}Z_{ab}^{l}=1]
=ℙ⁡[𝕊]∎\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}[{\mathbb{S}}]\qed

Retaining information

We will first prove the complexity bound Lemma 5.1 for the task of retaining the initial node feature: fv​(G)=𝑿vf_{v}({G})={\bm{X}}_{v}.

See 5.1

Proof.

Note that for r≥2r\geq 2, 𝑰a​b<1{{\bm{I}}}_{ab}<1 for all nodes a,b∈𝒱Ga,b\in{\mathcal{V}_{G}} for all model architectures except the MLP. Then, with positive probability, all messages are lost in a layer ll, i.e., Za,bl=0Z_{a,b}^{l}=0 for all a,b∈𝒱Ga,b\in{\mathcal{V}_{G}}. Hence, only with probability ϕ<1\phi<1 any message is successful in layer ll. A necessary condition for retaining the initial node feature is that in every layer, at least one message is successful. Thereby, we have the following lower bound:

ℙ[lossyWLv(t(G))⊨f(G)]≤ϕL.\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}(t({G}))\vDash f({G})]\leq\phi^{L}.

It follows immediately, that

MPC​(ℳ,fv,G)≥L​log⁡(1/ϕ).∎{\textup{MPC}}({\mathcal{M}},f_{v},{G})\geq L\log(1/\phi).\qed

Propagating Information

We will now prove the complexity bound Lemma 5.2 for the task fv​(G)=𝑿uf_{v}({G})={\bm{X}}_{u} of propagating information from a source node uu to a target node vv at distance D=dG​(u,v)D=d_{G}(u,v).

See 5.2

Proof.

Trivially, for the MLP baseline and D>0D>0, we have:

MPCMLP​(fv,G)=∞.{\textup{MPC}}_{\text{MLP}}(f_{v},{G})=\infty.

For GCN-VN, notice that each original node in G~{\tilde{{G}}} has degree r+2r+2 (rr neighbors in the input graph, the self-loop, and the connection to the virtual node) and the virtual node has degree 1/n1/n. It is easy to see that for D=0D=0 and D=1D=1, the minimal depth required to solve this task is L=0L=0 and L=1L=1, respectively. Trivially, the MPC complexities for these cases are 0 and log⁡(r+2)\log(r+2). Both are ≤2​log⁡(n)\leq 2\log(n).

For D≥2D\geq 2, the minimal depth required to solve this tasks is L=2L=2: One sufficient set of messages consists of the message from uu to the virtual node (which has probability of success 1/n1/n) and from the virtual node to vv (which has probability of success 1/(r+2)1/(r+2)). By Lemma C.10, this implies

MPCGCN-VN​(fv,G)≤log⁡(n⁡(r+2)).{\textup{MPC}}_{\text{GCN-VN}}(f_{v},{G})\leq\log(n(r+2)).

And hence,

MPCGCN-VN​(fv,G)≤2​log⁡(n).{\textup{MPC}}_{\text{GCN-VN}}(f_{v},{G})\leq 2\log(n).

For all other MPNNs, notice that the probability that G,v∼𝒢𝒱{G},v\sim{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}} contains a cycle where every node is in the DD-hop neighborhood around vv approaches 0 as n→∞n\to\infty for a given DD. Hence, we can choose nn such that this probability is ≤ϵ\leq\epsilon for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

Then, we can bound the expected complexity by (as MPC is always non-negative):

𝔼G,v∼𝒢𝒱​[MPCℳ​(fv,G)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{G},v\sim{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}}[{\textup{MPC}}_{\mathcal{M}}(f_{v},G)]
≥ℙ⁡[no cycle around v]⋅𝔼G,v∼𝒢𝒱​[MPCℳ​(fv,G)∣no cycle around v]\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{P}[\text{no cycle around $v$}]\cdot\mathbb{E}_{{G},v\sim{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}}[{\textup{MPC}}_{\mathcal{M}}(f_{v},G)\mid\text{no cycle around $v$}]
=(1−ϵ)⋅𝔼G,v∼𝒢𝒱​[MPCℳ​(fv,G)∣no cycle around v]\displaystyle=(1-\epsilon)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{{G},v\sim{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}}[{\textup{MPC}}_{\mathcal{M}}(f_{v},G)\mid\text{no cycle around $v$}]

where "no cycle around vv" denotes the event that there is no cycle where every node is in the DD-hop neighborhood around vv.

Next, we need to bound 𝔼G,v∼𝒢𝒱​[MPCℳ​(fv,G)∣no cycle around v]\mathbb{E}_{{G},v\sim{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}}[{\textup{MPC}}_{\mathcal{M}}(f_{v},G)\mid\text{no cycle around $v$}]. For this, we will show that MPCℳ​(fv,G)≥log⁡((r+1)L){\textup{MPC}}_{\mathcal{M}}(f_{v},G)\geq\log((r+1)^{L}) for any G,v∈𝒢𝒱{G},v\in{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}} without a cycle around vv. It is easy to see that for all considered MPNNs without a virtual node, the minimal depth required to solve this task is then L=DL=D. Then, a necessary set of messages consists of the messages on the only (as there is no cycle around vv) DD-length path from uu to vv. Each message on this path has a success probability ≤1/(r+1)\leq 1/(r+1). By Lemma C.11, this implies:

MPCℳ​(fv,G)≥log⁡((r+1)D){\textup{MPC}}_{\mathcal{M}}(f_{v},G)\geq\log((r+1)^{D})

Finally, by choosing ϵ\epsilon small enough, we have

𝔼G,v∼𝒢𝒱​[MPCℳ​(fv,G)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{G},v\sim{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}}[{\textup{MPC}}_{\mathcal{M}}(f_{v},G)]
≥(1−ϵ)⋅𝔼G,v∼𝒢𝒱​[MPCℳ​(fv,G)∣no cycle around v]\displaystyle\geq(1-\epsilon)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{{G},v\sim{{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{V}}}}[{\textup{MPC}}_{\mathcal{M}}(f_{v},G)\mid\text{no cycle around $v$}]
≥(1−ϵ)⋅log⁡((r+1)D)\displaystyle\geq(1-\epsilon)\cdot\log((r+1)^{D})
≥D​log⁡(r)∎\displaystyle\geq D\log(r)\qed

Extracting topological information

Lastly, we consider the ring transfer task. To simplify notations here, we will consider the complexity of fv​(G)=𝑿uf_{v}({G})={\bm{X}}_{u} for a single node uu on the cycle of size ss that vv is part of. The tasks involve 1) identifying that uu is part of the cycle 2) propagating the node feature information from uu to vv. We will now prove the complexity bounds in Lemma 5.3:

Lemma C.12.

Assume LL is the minimal depth required to solve the task fv​(G)=𝐗uf_{v}({G})={\bm{X}}_{u} with architecture ℳ{\mathcal{M}} where uu is a node on the cycle of size ss that vv is part of. Further assume that there is only a single cycle in the ⌈s/2⌉\lceil s/2\rceil-hop neighborhood of vv. Then, the expected MPC complexities are:

For CIN & FragNet:O(log(sr))For GSN:≤⌈s/2⌉log(r+1)For all others:≥slog(r)\text{For CIN \& FragNet:}\>\>O(\log(sr))\quad\quad\text{For GSN:}\>\>\leq\lceil s/2\rceil\log(r+1)\quad\quad\text{For all others:}\>\>\geq s\log(r)
Proof.

FragNet: Notice that for FragNet L=2L=2 is the minimal depth required to solve this task. With L=2L=2 a sufficient set of messages involves a message from uu to the fragment node that represents this cycle (with message success probability 1/s1/s) and from the fragment node to vv (with message success probability 1/(r+2)1/(r+2)). Using Lemma C.10, the bound follows immediately.

CIN: Again, for CIN L=2L=2 is the minimal depth required to solve this task. A sufficient set of messages involves a message from the ring node (which contains as initial encoding all node features from the nodes in the ring) to an edge node. And from the edge node to vv. Notice that the edge node has degree s+2s+2 (an edge to every other edge node in the cycle, an edge to the ring node and two edges to the original nodes) and vv has degree 2​r+12r+1 (edges to all rr neighboring nodes in G{G}, edges to corresponding edge nodes, and self-loop). Hence, we have message success probabilities 1/(s+2)1/(s+2) and 1/(2​r+1)1/(2r+1). Again, using Lemma C.10, the bound follows immediately.

GSN: Notice that for GSN the cycle information is already contained in the initial node-feature. So the task is simply to propagate the node feature information to vv for a distance of at most ⌈s/2⌉\lceil s/2\rceil. Hence, a sufficient set of messages consists of the messages on a path of length L≤⌈s/2⌉L\leq\lceil s/2\rceil from uu to vv, each with success probability 1/(r+1)1/(r+1). Again, using Lemma C.10, the bound follows immediately.

All other MPNNs: For all other MPNNs, the minimum depth required to solve this task is L=sL=s (for L<sL<s, it is impossible to detect the cycle). It is easy to see that in order to identify the cycle at node vv, there needs to be a set of successful messages going around the full cycle returning to vv. Or more formally, for a cycle consisting of nodes v,a1,a2,…,as−1,vv,a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{s-1},v, we define two possible message traversal patterns:

Cycle↻:=Zv​a11=1∧Za1​a22=1∧Za2​a33=1∧⋯∧Zas−1​vs=1\text{Cycle}_{\circlearrowright}:=Z_{va_{1}}^{1}=1\land Z_{a_{1}a_{2}}^{2}=1\land Z_{a_{2}a_{3}}^{3}=1\land\cdots\land Z_{a_{s-1}v}^{s}=1

and

Cycle↺:=Zv​as−11=1∧Zas−1​as−22=1∧Zas−2​as−33=1∧⋯∧Za1​vs=1.\text{Cycle}_{\circlearrowleft}:=Z_{va_{s-1}}^{1}=1\land Z_{a_{s-1}a_{s-2}}^{2}=1\land Z_{a_{s-2}a_{s-3}}^{3}=1\land\cdots\land Z_{a_{1}v}^{s}=1.

Additionally, node vv must retain its unique node feature throughout all LL layers to recognize that the returning messages originated from itself.33 3 A sufficient condition for this task would be even stronger, requiring all nodes in the cycle to retain their features until the messages through the cycle reach them. Hence, a necessary condition for lossyWLv​(G)⊨fv​(G)\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash f_{v}({G}) is

Zv​v1=1∧Zv​v2=1∧⋯∧Zv​vs=1∧(Cycle↻∨Cycle↺).Z_{vv}^{1}=1\land Z_{vv}^{2}=1\land\cdots\land Z_{vv}^{s}=1\land(\text{Cycle}_{\circlearrowright}\lor\text{Cycle}_{\circlearrowleft}).

Therefore, we have

ℙ[lossyWLv(G)⊨fv(G)]≤ℙ[Zv​v1=1∧Zv​v2=1∧⋯∧Zv​vs=1∧(Cycle↻∨Cycle↺)].\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash f_{v}({G})]\leq\mathbb{P}[Z_{vv}^{1}=1\land Z_{vv}^{2}=1\land\cdots\land Z_{vv}^{s}=1\land(\text{Cycle}_{\circlearrowright}\lor\text{Cycle}_{\circlearrowleft})].

Notice that ℙ⁡[Za​bl]=1/(r+1)\mathbb{P}[Z_{ab}^{l}]=1/(r+1) for any message, as every node has degree rr and the additonal self-loop. Then, because of the independence of all Za​blZ_{ab}^{l}, we have

ℙ[lossyWLv(G)⊨fv(G)]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[\textup{lossyWL}_{v}({G})\vDash f_{v}({G})] ≤ℙ[Zv​v1=1∧Zv​v2=1∧⋯∧Zv​vs=1∧(Cycle↻∨Cycle↺)].\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}[Z_{vv}^{1}=1\land Z_{vv}^{2}=1\land\cdots\land Z_{vv}^{s}=1\land(\text{Cycle}_{\circlearrowright}\lor\text{Cycle}_{\circlearrowleft})].
=ℙ[Zv​v1=1∧Zv​v2=1∧⋯∧Zv​vs=1]⋅ℙ[Cycle↻∨Cycle↺]\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}[Z_{vv}^{1}=1\land Z_{vv}^{2}=1\land\cdots\land Z_{vv}^{s}=1]\cdot\mathbb{P}[\text{Cycle}_{\circlearrowright}\lor\text{Cycle}_{\circlearrowleft}]
≤1/2⋅ℙ[Cycle↻∨Cycle↺)]\displaystyle\leq 1/2\cdot\mathbb{P}[\text{Cycle}_{\circlearrowright}\lor\text{Cycle}_{\circlearrowleft})]
≤1/2⋅2⋅ℙ⁡[Cycle↻]\displaystyle\leq 1/2\cdot 2\cdot\mathbb{P}[\text{Cycle}_{\circlearrowright}]
=(1r+1)s.\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{r+1}\right)^{s}.

While this bound is not tight (we’ve made several relaxations), it is sufficient to establish the ≥s​log⁡(r)\geq s\log(r) MPC complexity lower bound.

MLP: The complexity is trivially infinite. ∎

Lastly, we give a short proof why WLC is 00 for this task. For this, we generally show that for graphs with unique node features any (at least WL-expressive) architecture with at least one layer can distinguish all non-isomorphic graphs, and hence solve any task.

Lemma C.13.

Let 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} be a family of graphs with unique node features, i.e., for any G∈𝒢{G}\in{\mathcal{G}}, no two nodes v,w∈𝒱Gv,w\in{\mathcal{V}_{G}} have the same node features. Then the WL output after one iteration {{WLv1∣v∈𝒱G}}\{\mskip-5.0mu\{{\textup{WL}}_{v}^{1}\mid v\in{\mathcal{V}_{G}}\}\mskip-5.0mu\} differs for any two non-isomorphic graphs in 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}.

Proof.

Let G1,G2∈𝒢{G}_{1},{G}_{2}\in{\mathcal{G}} be two non-isomorphic graphs. Suppose, for contradiction, that the WL output after one iteration is the same for both graphs, i.e., {{WLv1∣v∈𝒱G1}}={{WLw1∣w∈𝒱G2}}\{\mskip-5.0mu\{{\textup{WL}}_{v}^{1}\mid v\in{\mathcal{V}_{G}}_{1}\}\mskip-5.0mu\}=\{\mskip-5.0mu\{{\textup{WL}}_{w}^{1}\mid w\in{\mathcal{V}_{G}}_{2}\}\mskip-5.0mu\} as multisets.

Since all node features in G1{G}_{1} and G2{G}_{2} are unique within each graph, the initial WL labels WLv0{\textup{WL}}_{v}^{0} are distinct for all nodes vv in each graph. After one iteration, each WLv1{\textup{WL}}_{v}^{1} consists of the node’s original feature combined with the multiset of its neighbors’ features, i.e., WLv1=(WLv0,{{WLu0∣u∈N⁡(v)}}){\textup{WL}}_{v}^{1}=\left({\textup{WL}}_{v}^{0},\{\mskip-5.0mu\{{\textup{WL}}_{u}^{0}\mid u\in{N}(v)\}\mskip-5.0mu\}\right).

Given that {{WLv1∣v∈𝒱G1}}={{WLw1∣w∈𝒱G2}}\{\mskip-5.0mu\{{\textup{WL}}_{v}^{1}\mid v\in{\mathcal{V}_{G}}_{1}\}\mskip-5.0mu\}=\{\mskip-5.0mu\{{\textup{WL}}_{w}^{1}\mid w\in{\mathcal{V}_{G}}_{2}\}\mskip-5.0mu\}, there must exist a bijection f:𝒱G1→𝒱G2f:{\mathcal{V}_{G}}_{1}\rightarrow{\mathcal{V}_{G}}_{2} such that WLv1=WLf⁡(v)1{\textup{WL}}_{v}^{1}={\textup{WL}}_{f(v)}^{1} for all v∈𝒱G1v\in{\mathcal{V}_{G}}_{1}.

This implies that for each v∈𝒱G1v\in{\mathcal{V}_{G}}_{1}: (1) WLv0=WLf⁡(v)0{\textup{WL}}_{v}^{0}={\textup{WL}}_{f(v)}^{0} (the original node features match), and (2) {{WLu0∣u∈N⁡(v)}}={{WLw0∣w∈N⁡(f⁡(v))}}\{\mskip-5.0mu\{{\textup{WL}}_{u}^{0}\mid u\in{N}(v)\}\mskip-5.0mu\}=\{\mskip-5.0mu\{{\textup{WL}}_{w}^{0}\mid w\in{N}(f(v))\}\mskip-5.0mu\} (the multisets of neighbor features match).

From (1), since node features are unique within each graph, ff maps each node in G1{G}_{1} to a unique node in G2{G}_{2} with identical features.

From (2), for each v∈𝒱G1v\in{\mathcal{V}_{G}}_{1}, there must exist a bijection gv:N⁡(v)→N⁡(f⁡(v))g_{v}:{N}(v)\rightarrow{N}(f(v)) such that WLu0=WLgv​(u)0{\textup{WL}}_{u}^{0}={\textup{WL}}_{g_{v}(u)}^{0} for all u∈N⁡(v)u\in{N}(v).

Due to the uniqueness of node features and (1), we must have gv​(u)=f​(u)g_{v}(u)=f(u) for all u∈N⁡(v)u\in{N}(v). This implies that for all v∈𝒱G1v\in{\mathcal{V}_{G}}_{1} and u∈𝒱G1u\in{\mathcal{V}_{G}}_{1}: u∈N⁡(v)⇔f⁡(u)∈N⁡(f⁡(v))u\in{N}(v)\iff f(u)\in{N}(f(v)) Therefore, ff is an isomorphism between G1{G}_{1} and G2{G}_{2}, contradicting our assumption that the graphs are non-isomorphic. Thus, the WL output after one iteration must differ for any two non-isomorphic graphs in 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}. ∎

Appendix D Additional results and Experimental Details

We present the following additional results:

  • •

    Extended figures showing all considered model architectures across all tasks.

  • •

    Robustness analysis demonstrating that MPC predictions hold across different hyperparameter choices (hidden dimensions) for the information retention task.

  • •

    Validation on Erdős-Rényi (ER) graphs, confirming that MPC accurately matches performance trends also on a different synthetic graph family.

  • •

    Real-world validation on graphs from ZINC [15] and peptides datasets [14] showing that MPC explains performance better than classical expressivity theory for real-world graph structures.

  • •

    Results showing that insight on synthetic proxy tasks can mirror performance trends on real-world benchmarks where the precise tasks are unknown.

Additionally, we carefully describe all experimental details and setups.

D.1 Implementation Details and Experimental Setup

We use pytorch [39] and torch-geometric [17] (released under an MIT license) for the implementation of all models. For optimization, we use the Adam optimizer [30]. The training, validation and test sets containing random rr-regular graphs are generated using networkx [24]. For all standard MPNNs we use their pytorch geometric implementation. Note that GSN [8] only specifies the additional node features and not the downstream MPNN. We use the most common MPNN, GCN, as downstream MPNN for all experiments for GSN. For CIN [5] we use our own implementation following exactly the method proposed in their paper. Additionally, for FragNet, we use a custom implementation of their FR-WL model without edge representations using a GCN as base MPNN. For CIN, GSN, and FragNet we use a fragmentation scheme identifying every cycle of size at most 6 (unless otherwise noted). For all models we use an initial feature embedding layer and a final output MLP. Additionally, we use BatchNorm [26] for normalization. We found little difference between learning rates in {0.001,0.005,0.01}\{0.001,0.005,0.01\} for all models and tasks. The shown results are for the learning rate 0.0050.005. We train all models for all settings using three different seeds for a maximum of 50 epochs, showing the average results. All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 GPUs with 16GB memory allocation per job. Training times vary by model architecture, ranging from 10-30 minutes. Monte Carlo simulations for complexity calculations run on a single Intel Xeon E5-2630 v4 CPU (2.20GHz) and complete in under 10 seconds. The peptides dataset of the lrgb [14] is released under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license. The ZINC dataset [15] is distributed under a custom license (free to use for everyone).

D.2 Retaining information

For the task fv​(G)=𝑿uf_{v}({G})={\bm{X}}_{u}, we randomly generate 33-regular graphs with n=50n=50 nodes where each node is randomly assigned to one of ten possible classes. We use a training set of size 2000, a validation set of size 500 and a test set of size 2000. We simulate the complexities using Monte Carlo simulation on 100 different graphs from the test set, and for each graph 1000 trials (with the same method explained in § D.3). Fig. 9 shows the accuracy and simulated MPC complexity for all considered model architectures. Additionally, Fig. 10 shows that the complexity measure is robust to changes in the hidden dimension hyperparameter, i.e., trends in MPC complexity align with empirical performance also for different hidden dimensions. Moreover, Fig. 11 shows how complexity and accuracy changes for different levels of sparsity.

Erdős–Rényi graphs

We repeat the retaining information experiment with Erdős–Rényi (ER) graphs with n=50n=50 nodes and node connection probability p=0.06p=0.06. Fig. 12 shows that generally, trends in MPC complexity align with trends in empirical performance (except for Sage and CIN, the two models that directly optimize the weight of the residual channel) as well for ER graphs.

D.3 Propagating Information

For the task fv​(G)=𝑿uf_{v}({G})={\bm{X}}_{u}, we randomly generate 3-regular graphs with n=50n=50 nodes. In each graph, we randomly select a target node vv. For a given distance DD, we select a node uu with distance DD from vv. Then, vv gets the unique label 00 identifying it as target node, uu is randomly assigned a target label in {1,…,10}\{1,\dots,10\}, and all other nodes get a random label from {11,…,20}\{11,\dots,20\}. For each distance DD, we use training sets of different sizes and a validation set of size 500 and a test set of size 2000. We simulate the complexities using Monte Carlo simulation on 100 different graphs from the test set, and for each graph 1000 trials. Fig. 13 shows the average test accuracy by training data size and Fig. 14 shows the test accuracy and the complexity for the dataset size 1000.

Erdős–Rényi graphs

Again, we repeat the information propagation experiment with ER graphs with n=50n=50 nodes and node connection probability p=0.04p=0.04. Fig. 15 show that trends in MPC complexity align with trends in empirical performance as well for ER graphs.

Peptides dataset

Additionally, we repeat the information propagation task on graphs from the real-world peptides-func/peptides-struct dataset. It comprises larger peptide molecules that require models to consider long-range interactions [14]. Therefore, the information propagation task, testing the models’ ability to exchange information over varying distances, is particularly well-suited for this dataset.

Similar to our approach for random regular and ER graphs, we randomly select one node of each graph in the dataset as target node vv. For a given distance DD, we randomly select a node uu with distance DD from vv as the source node. Then, vv gets the unique label 00 identifying it as target node, uu is randomly assigned a label in {1,…,10}\{1,\dots,10\}, and all other nodes get a random label from {11,…,20}\{11,\dots,20\}. We then randomly sample different numbers of graphs from the dataset as train graphs. In summary, this allows us to analyze and isolate the information propagation capability of models on real-world graphs requiring long-range interactions.

Fig. 17 shows again a connection between sample complexity needed to achieve perfect accuracy and MPC complexity, underlining that MPC is also a good predictor of performance for graph topologies occurring in the real world.

D.4 Extracting topological information

For the ring transfer task, we use randomly generated 44-regular graphs with n=50n=50 nodes conditioned on having a cycle of size ss at a node vv (and no smaller cycle). Each node is randomly assigned a unique label in {1,…,50}\{1,\dots,50\}. The multilabel classification task fv​(G)f_{v}({G}) is then to classify which labels between 1 and 50 are part of the cycle that contains vv. For each cycle size, we generate training sets of varying size, a validation set of size 1000 and a test set of size 10000. For GSN, FragNet, and CIN we use a fragmentation scheme identifying cycles of size at most 5. For all models, we use the minimal number of layers with which they can solve all tasks: for FragNet and CIN: 2, for all other models: 5. For CIN and FragNet, we explicitly compute the complexities. For all other models, we use the bounds provided in Lemma 5.3. All results show the binary average precision. Fig. 18 shows the average precision and complexities for this task for the maximal dataset size of 10000. Additionally, Fig. 19 shows the average precision in relation to dataset size.

Erdős–Rényi graphs

Again, we repeat the ring transfer task with ER graphs with n=50n=50 nodes and edge probability p=0.04p=0.04 conditioned on having a ring of size ss at node vv. The label assignment is done in the same way as for the random regular graphs. Fig. 20 shows that complexities also align with MPC complexities for ER graphs.

ZINC dataset

We additionally test the ring transfer capabilities of the models on real-world graphs from the ZINC molecular regression dataset [15]. The ZINC dataset comprises small molecules and the benchmark task is to predict the penalized logP score which involves the number of cycles. Therefore the graphs from the ZINC dataset are well-suited to test our models cycle detection capabilities. For this, we first filter all graphs to contain rings of size ss. Second, we randomly choose a node vv that is part of cycle ss for each graph. The labels are assigned in the same way as for the random regular graphs and the ER graphs.

Figs. 22 and 23 show that trends in MPC complexity align again with empirical performance. Again, the superior performance of GSN, CIN, and FragNet cannot be explained by their increased iso expressivity(WLC 0 for all MPNNs) but by their reduced MPC due to their cycle-oriented inductive bias.

Additionally, we compare results on the synthetic ring transfer task to empirical performance on the standard ZINC molecular property prediction task (penalized logP), where ring identification is crucial for accurate predictions. As shown in Tab. 2, trends in MPC on the synthetic ring task match trends in empirical performance on ZINC: architectures with lower ring detection complexity (GSN, FragNet, CIN) significantly outperform standard MPNNs on both tasks. This demonstrates that MPC analysis of targeted proxy tasks can provide valuable insights into real-world performance, even when exact target functions are unknown or complexity values are computationally infeasible to derive.

D.5 Simulation of Complexities

We show in Algorithm 1 for the exemplary task of propagating information from a source node uu to a target node vv how the complexities can be efficiently simulated using Monte Carlo simulation.
